A coding agent refines selected harnesses using archived code, execution feedback, and a library of reusable harness mechanisms. With 15 refinement attempts per benchmark, HarnessFlow achieves the highest mean test scores among the compared methods on six benchmarks spanning agentic tasks, coding, and web interaction. The optimized harnesses achieve an average score of 69.48%, outperforming the initial harnesses and Meta-Harness by 10.89 and 3.95 percentage points, respectively, while incurring lower average per-task execution costs than hand-engineered baselines. These results suggest that structured harness search offers a promising route toward automating the design of capable and efficient LLM agents.

papers.title: Learning Noise Optimization for Reward Alignment in Few-Step Generative Models
papers.abstract: Reward alignment for diffusion- and flow-based generative models is often formulated over stochastic trajectories, making it less suitable for few-step deterministic generators. Initial noise optimization provides a trajectory-free alternative, but existing gradient-free methods require costly per-sample search at inference. We introduce LeNO (Learning Noise Optimization), which amortizes reward-guided initial noise optimization into a learned residual transport while keeping the pretrained generator frozen. LeNO learns an anchor-conditioned distribution over noise corrections using Local GRPO and scalar rewards, eliminating iterative test-time optimization. For Gaussian initial noise with norm-preserving projection, we derive a tractable upper bound on the KL divergence between the corrected noise distribution and the original prior, providing a principled regularization objective. We evaluate LeNO on few-step text-to-image and protein structure generation, including expensive black-box designability rewards. Across both domains, LeNO improves target rewards with a single noise correction at inference while largely preserving generation quality and diversity.

papers.title: From the quantum group $U_{q^{1/2}}( {\widehat {\mathfrak{sl}}}_2 )$ to the Kronecker quantum cluster algebra
papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal A_q$ be the Kronecker quantum cluster algebra with principal coefficients. We construct an explicit algebra homomorphism from the whole quantum group ${U_{q^{1/2}}}( {\widehat {\mathfrak{sl}_2}} )$ to $\mathcal A_q$, whose images together with either of the two frozen variables generate $\mathcal A_q$. As an application, we obtain algebra homomorphisms from the split $\imath$quantum groups of affine $\widehat {\mathfrak{sl}}_2$ to $\mathcal A_q$. Moreover, we explicitly determine the images of the positive and negative real and imaginary root vectors of ${U_{q^{1/2}}}( {\widehat {\mathfrak{sl}_2}} )$ in terms of quantum cluster variables.

papers.title: Analysis of Local Open-Weight LLM Agents on Vulnerability-Reproduction Tasks
papers.abstract: Open-weight language models that fit on a single consumer GPU are becoming capable on a growing range of tasks, and they matter because they can run locally without sending the code to a hosted service. Vulnerability reproduction, turning a vulnerability description into an input that crashes the vulnerable build, is a natural target for them, since it is an automated analysis task closer to test generation than to code comprehension and it runs against a build that must be executed rather than read. In order to assess whether current models can perform it, we evaluate twelve configurations of local models, spanning three generations, two architectures and three quantization levels, on ten CyberGym vulnerability-reproduction tasks, three runs each under one harness, and release the full artefact. We show that every configuration, down to the 4B model, solves most of the six easier tasks, and configurations separate only on the remaining four. For the harder tasks, the 27B model is required. Quantization did not change what the models solved in any matched pair, but it changed how fast they got there, and the mixture of experts reached the same scores in less wall clock. We also examine the agent trajectories. Almost every run we examined, including those that fail, names the vulnerable function and states the correct hypothesis, and what separates a solved task from an unsolved one is whether that hypothesis becomes a working input.

papers.title: CrossPressor: Scalable Cross-View Fusion for Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) becomes increasingly difficult to scale to long multi-view sequences. Anchor-based compression methods such as ZPressor alleviate representation growth by decoding Gaussians only from a compact set of anchor feature maps, but keeping these anchors fixed forces each one to aggregate an increasing number of support views. We identify this representation--fusion mismatch and introduce \textbf{CrossPressor}, a training-free method for scalable anchor-based fusion. CrossPressor preserves all decoder-facing anchor queries while constraining the view-growing support sequence through coverage-cycled evidence routing, distributing retained spatial evidence across support views and fusion layers while keeping all support views represented. Routing before K/V projection, together with joint context packing, further reduces support-side fusion cost without retraining. CrossPressor maintains reconstruction quality close to dense fusion while achieving up to $26.12\times$ faster cross-view fusion and $1.43\times$ end-to-end acceleration on long input sequences. Our project page is at: https://yuhsihu.github.io/CrossPressor.

papers.title: A Systematic Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Personalized Reasoning of Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: People often make decisions by holistically reasoning over heterogeneous forms of personal information. In this paper, we study the relatively underexplored capability of multimodal personalized reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To this end, we introduce \texttt{MPRBench}, a novel and comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate personalized reasoning across a wide range of tasks and real-world challenges. \texttt{MPRBench} consists of 12 sub-tasks and additionally supports interpretable analysis of representative error cases. Through extensive experiments, we find that current personalized MLLMs still struggle with personalized reasoning due to several key challenges, including inaccurate recognition of personalized concepts and sensitivity to irrelevant personal information. We hope that MPRBench will stimulate further research on personalized reasoning in MLLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/kkdh15/MPRBench

papers.title: Connection of surface code patches based on entanglement distillation without postselection
papers.abstract: Distributed quantum computing is a promising approach for overcoming the scalability limitations of fault-tolerant quantum computing. Entanglement distillation, a process that extracts higher-fidelity entangled states from noisy ones, plays a key role in distributed quantum computing. However, simple distillation protocols typically rely on postselection, which poses practical challenges for implementation. Here, we propose a scheme for distributed surface-code quantum computing that benefits from entanglement distillation even without postselection. Numerical simulations show that the logical error rates in the proposed scheme are lower than those in the setting without distillation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the logical error rates can be suppressed further by exploiting the asymmetry between spacelike and timelike errors in the surface code. The proposed scheme offers a practical and simple approach to distributed quantum computing with surface codes.

papers.title: Homology and Topology of Partially Ordered Fields
papers.abstract: We develop a unified homology theory for directed partial orders (DPOs) and lattice-ordered positive cones on fields of characteristic zero. With the underlying field and its operations fixed, we define order?carrying spaces independently by topological conditions, establish a bijection with DPO positive cones, and characterize lattice orders by intersections of minimal open neighborhoods. A unified comparison theorem identifies graded Ext for region ideals with sheaf cohomology and multiplicative Tor with the reduced singular homology of truncated regions, giving a topological interpretation of the existence and preservation of reduced decompositions. We obtain canonical cohomological obstructions to lattice ordering, prove that a coefficient module for positive multiplication is flat if and only if the multiplier has a positive inverse, and show that every strict extension of positive cones on the same field produces a nonzero first Tor obstruction. Finally, we place the concrete lattice recently constructed by Bao-Zhang within this framework.

papers.title: SonoDyno: A Sonic Dynamometer for Engine Speed and Load Estimation from Audio
papers.abstract: Controllable engine sound synthesis, Active Sound Design and engine order analysis all build on the relationship between the sound of an engine and its momentary operating state: its speed and its load. Recordings of engine sound are abundant in archives, sample packs and online video, yet they rarely carry time-aligned annotations of that state, which limits their applicability to controllable engine sound generation. We present SonoDyno, which estimates the engine speed, the cylinder count and an engine-normalized load intensity from a microphone signal alone, with no tachometer, no bus access and no prior knowledge of the engine configuration. A convolutional scorer of 124,302 parameters reads the harmonic order energy of each frame at three time-frequency resolutions to jointly score cylinder count and speed, and a decoder imposes the rotational dynamics of the engine on the speed trajectory. A second head estimates the load intensity, the position of the torque between the engine's drag floor at 0 and its full-load ceiling at 1, from the order levels at the decoded speed. On recordings of engines it has never heard, with microphone position, engine type and cylinder count unknown, SonoDyno places 93 to 97% of the frames within 2% of the true speed, identifies the cylinder count with 80% accuracy and confuses the octave on fewer than 2% of the frames. On an unseen engine of a known type, the load intensity has a mean absolute error of 0.12, and the sign of the torque, driving or braking, is right on 91% of the frames. General pitch trackers fall behind even when the harmonic order of each engine is supplied: on our validation recordings and at a tolerance of 5%, the best of them places 62% of the frames within the tolerance, against 96% for SonoDyno.

papers.title: CLEAR: Structured Specifications for Controllable Long-Horizon ML Research Engineering
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly being used to automate machine learning (ML) research workflows, ranging from code development and experiment execution to research reproduction and scientific discovery. Recent systems demonstrate that LLMs can perform substantial portions of ML research engineering with limited human intervention. These advances suggest a shift from automating individual research tasks toward automating long-horizon workflows that transform research artifacts into executable ML systems. However, ML research engineering remains substantially more difficult than isolated code generation. A research artifact typically specifies a system only implicitly through a mixture of natural-language descriptions, equations, pseudo-code, implementation details, datasets, and evaluation protocols. An agent must first infer the intended computational structure, translate it into executable components, coordinate their dependencies, and repeatedly diagnose and repair failures during execution. Consequently, the quality of the final system depends not only on code generation, but also on whether the agent can maintain a consistent representation of what should be implemented throughout this long-horizon process.

papers.title: A brief overview of the baryon cycle in galaxies
papers.abstract: Galaxy formation and evolution is governed by the continuous exchange of gas between the cosmic web, the circumgalactic medium (CGM), and the interstellar medium (ISM) of galaxies. This brief review summarises our current understanding of this baryon cycle, from the accretion of gas onto galaxies to its conversion into stars, and the feedback processes that regulate the growth of galaxies. Several open questions will be highlighted, that will encourage progresses in cosmological simulations, multiwavelength observations, and theory to resolve.

papers.title: Learning Pseudo-Riemannian Manifolds for Heterophilic Graphs via Graph Signature
papers.abstract: Several widely used families of Graph Neural Networks carry a positive-definite geometric prior. Graph convolution read as heat diffusion needs a positive semi-definite operator, hyperbolic models place features on positive-definite Riemannian manifolds, and dot-product and GAT-style attention scores use positive-definite inner products. On heterophilic graphs, where edges often signify dissimilarity or structural repulsion, that prior is a mismatch: no positive-definite form can assign a negative squared distance to a direction the labels separate. To measure the mismatch, we introduce the Graph Signature Index ($s_{\mathcal{G}}$), the inertia of a class-compatibility matrix built from label topology alone, and we prove that no value of the edge or node homophily index in $(0,1)$ rules out a negative eigenvalue. We then propose the Pseudo-Riemannian Attention Network (PRAT), whose attention logit is a signed squared pseudo-distance under a learnable diagonal metric initialized from $s_{\mathcal{G}}$. The design is diagnose-then-learn: the signature supplies a sign structure that unconstrained training keeps outside near-zero directions, and the projection learns the rest of the metric around it. Across fifteen node-classification benchmarks PRAT outperforms or matches the strongest heterophily-adapted models. A controlled ablation ties that performance to the sign structure itself: with architecture and protocol fixed, forbidding the metric to be indefinite costs accuracy on the graphs $s_{\mathcal{G}}$ marks as indefinite and leaves the others unchanged.

papers.title: Online Bayesian Inference for a Dirichlet Process Mixture of Binary Logit Models
papers.abstract: Flexible travel behaviour models for preference heterogeneity have largely remained within the batch-estimation paradigm. The growing availability of continuously collected behavioural data, for example from smartphone applications, highlights the need for methods that update posterior inference on such heterogeneity as new observations arrive. This study proposes an online Bayesian inference method for a Dirichlet process mixture of binary logit models. The main challenge is to update the posterior as observations arrive while allowing the latent cluster structure to expand and historical cluster assignments to be revised. We develop a sequential Monte Carlo sampler using a sequence of Pólya--Gamma-augmented partial-data posteriors, local particle-weight corrections, and recursively maintained sufficient statistics. Each observation's contribution can be added, removed, or replaced in these summaries, supporting both sequential coefficient updating and rejuvenation that revisits historical cluster assignments. The simulation study shows that observation-by-observation sequential updating yields final posterior summaries close to those obtained by batch Markov chain Monte Carlo. Sensitivity analyses further demonstrate trade-offs between posterior approximation accuracy and computational cost as the number of particles and rejuvenation settings are varied. An illustrative empirical application shows how the method tracks posterior evolution and produces observation-specific provisional posterior summaries with low latency as real-world trip records are processed sequentially. The proposed approach provides a methodological foundation for online inference in travel behaviour models with parameter heterogeneity and for future extensions to richer choice structures, low-latency decision support, and online anomaly screening.

papers.title: Retrials in Loss Systems: Mean-Field Analysis, Erlang Bounds, and Power-of-$d$ Comparison
papers.abstract: We consider a system of $N$ parallel, homogeneous servers, each with finite capacity $C$. Jobs requiring one unit of capacity arrive according to a Poisson process with total rate $Nλ$ and have exponential service times with rate $μ$. We study a decentralized random--retrial policy with $d$ attempts: upon arrival, a job is assigned to a uniformly chosen server; if the server is full, the job is reassigned to another uniformly chosen server, for at most $d$ attempts; if all $d$ attempts fail, the job is rejected. In the mean-field limit, we prove that the stationary blocking probability is characterized by the unique solution of a fixed-point equation involving the Erlang-B loss function, and we establish global convergence of the fluid model to this equilibrium. We also compare the mean-field stationary blocking probability with the analogous quantity in the power-of-$d$ model under the same parameters $(C,λ,μ)$. For the same $d$, we show, via coupling techniques, that the blocking probability under power-of-$d$ is always less than or equal to the blocking under retrial-of-$d$; but if we consider $d$ and $\tilde d$ with $\tilde d>d$, then the retrial-of-$\tilde d$ policy achieves a strictly lower blocking than the power-of-$d$ policy when $ρ=λ/μ$ is sufficiently large. Moreover we show that for some specific cases, like $C=2$, $d=2$ and $\tilde d=3$, it occurs for all $ρ>0$, not only for $ρ$ sufficiently large. We complement the analysis with simulations that estimate the load level above which retrial-of-$\tilde d$ outperforms power-of-$d$ in terms of blocking.

papers.title: Beyond Identity Creation: Bilinear Sybil Cost in Identities and Time
papers.abstract: Sybil defenses price the creation of an identity, yet influence goes, again and again, to active identities. We study the cost of maintaining influence. A defense has a bilinear Sybil cost with ratio $A$ if keeping $s$ identities active for $T$ periods costs at least $sT/A$ honest units: the average cost per identity-window is at least $1/A$ times an honest participant's cost. Recurrence alone does not guarantee this cost. The cost can be carried over from earlier periods, shared among many identities, or be negligible when fast hardware does the work of thousands of honest devices. We give four sufficient conditions for a defense that checks every identity each period to achieve bilinear Sybil cost: identity binding, freshness, a shared deadline, and sequential, non-batchable work. They yield two guarantees: a bilinear total cost, with $A$ the speed advantage of the adversary's fastest hardware, and, because the work must be fresh and finished by a common deadline, a bound on the identities active in a period by the processors running at that time. We prove that none of the four follows from the other three. A verifiable delay function on an identity-bound input meets all four without payments, with $A$ of 2 to 8 for CPUs and about 28 for a hypothetical ASIC, against $10^3$ to $10^7$ for hash puzzles. We measure one active identity per core per period against about 80,000 under a signed heartbeat, no gain from batching up to 1,000 identities, and rejection of all tested attacks.

papers.title: Small 5-chromatic unit-distance graphs in disks of radius 3/2, 5/4 and 23/20
papers.abstract: We give three explicit unit-distance graphs in the plane with chromatic number 5 whose vertices lie in small disks: a graph with 773 vertices inside an open disk of radius 3/2, one with 5713 vertices inside an open disk of radius 5/4, and one with 8168 vertices inside an open disk of radius 23/20. The smallest examples previously reported for these radii have 11725, 11725 and 31171 vertices. All coordinates are exact elements of Q(sqrt3, sqrt5, sqrt11). In each case 5-chromaticity is certified by an explicit 5-colouring and a DRAT proof that no 4-colouring exists. The 773-vertex graph is vertex-critical.

papers.title: NextGAN: Towards Simple and Scalable GAN Training for Image and Video Generation
papers.abstract: Adversarial training enables one- and few-step image and video generation, but conventional adversarial losses supervise critic values without directly specifying the gradients used to update the generator. We present NEXTGAN, which trains a scalar critic by regressing its input gradient onto displacements between independently paired reference and generated features at interpolated locations in frozen representation spaces. For a fixed generator, this regression is equivalent to an adversarial objective with a gradient-energy penalty, while the generator retains the standard potential-based GAN update. The same objective adapts pre-trained image and video generators with up to 14B parameters, without auxiliary losses, online teacher scores, or trajectories. On ImageNet $256 \times 256$, NEXTGAN achieves one-step FIDs of 2.87 with pixel-space JiT-B and 1.54 with latent-space DiT-XL/1; its adversarial form further reaches 1.36. For text-to-video generation, a single trained Wan2.1-1.3B model supports one-, two-, and four-step sampling, achieving the highest VBench total scores among the compared 1.3B methods at one and two steps. At two steps, NEXTGAN scores 83.13, exceeding rCM and AnyFlow by 1.25 and 0.47 points, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/LINs-lab/NextGAN.git.

papers.title: Consistency Learning and Distillation for One-Step MIMO-OFDM Channel Estimation
papers.abstract: Iterative neural channel estimators can improve recovery under pilot contamination, but repeated network evaluations increase inference cost. This paper develops observation-anchored consistency and Consistency Mid-Training (CMT) estimators for one-step channel estimation in multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) systems. Both estimators refine pilot-derived least-squares channel estimates in the delay-beam domain. Consistency learning couples endpoint predictions along noisy-to-clean paths. CMT then refines a compact consistency-trained student to predict a flow-matching teacher's endpoint from intermediate trajectory states. Across the evaluated SNR range, the compact CMT student reduces uncoded symbol error rate (SER) by 9.6-20.2% relative to the one-step flow-matching baseline (0.44-0.98 dB in logarithmic SER reduction), while using 74.5% fewer parameters and 73.0% fewer network multiply-accumulates.

papers.title: Evaluating Human-LLM Alignment on Visualization Preference
papers.abstract: There are often multiple valid visualizations, spanning different chart types, visual encodings, and aesthetic choices, that can all support a user's goal of analyzing a dataset. Determining which of these candidate visualizations is most appropriate, however, remains challenging. Prior work has leveraged expert-curated taxonomies to guide visualization design and subsequent quality evaluation, a practical evaluation model must also account for human-centric factors. Latest visualization tools integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate and refine visualizations, using LLM-as-a-judge to provide design feedback. Without a deeper understanding of whether, and in what ways, human and LLM perceptions of visualizations align, there is a real risk of deploying low-quality agents that do not reflect human judgment. We study this question through a pilot experiment - we formulate the problem as a preference task over curated chart pairs and compare the judgments of state-of-the-art vision models with those of a panel of human annotators. We establish a cautionary tale: such judges risk filtering out informative, compelling displays. We find that frontier models collapse human subjectivity, a rich signal that reveals contrasting design choices, into near-deterministic verdicts.

papers.title: Quo Vadis, Driving Scene Reconstruction? Occlusion-Aware Gaussian Densification
papers.abstract: While recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting methods enable efficient driving-scene reconstruction from surround-view images, their reliance on a single observation fundamentally hinders novel-view synthesis. Regions occluded in the input can become visible from novel viewpoints, leaving the reconstructed Gaussians under-constrained and incomplete. Moving beyond image-space inpainting for rendered views, we introduce OccSplat, a feed-forward framework whose core contribution is Occlusion-Aware Gaussian Densification, explicitly targeting missing scene geometry rather than missing pixels. By predicting new Gaussian primitives for unsupported regions, OccSplat completes the scene directly in the 3D representation. Specifically, OccSplat first identifies occluded regions that lack Gaussian support through Gaussian Occlusion Mapping. Gaussian Occlusion Completion then generates new primitives for these regions. The predicted primitives are integrated into the original representation to improve novel-view synthesis while retaining feed-forward inference without per-scene optimization. Experiments on the nuScenes benchmark demonstrate that OccSplat improves on the compared methods and yields particularly large gains in occluded regions, leading to more accurate and visually coherent driving-scene reconstruction.

papers.title: Quantitatively Probing the Tilt Angle Failures in 4D-STEM Polarisation Analysis
papers.abstract: Four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) is increasingly used to map polarisation in ferroic textures such as domain walls, vortices, merons and skyrmions. These textures are accompanied by local strain, lattice rotation and misorientation, which also modulate the diffraction features used to infer polar order. Even small deviations from the zone axis can therefore produce contrast that is indistinguishable from a polarisation signal. Here we quantify the tilt sensitivity of two polarisation-sensitive signals, diffraction disc intensity and Kikuchi band intensity, in three ferroelectrics with distinct polar distortions: PbTiO3, BaTiO3 and Cu3B7O13Cl boracite. We find that tilts of only 0.01-0.05 degrees reverse most Friedel-pair disc asymmetries, and even the most robust disc pairs reverse by 0.04 degrees in BaTiO3, 0.14 degrees in PbTiO3 and 0.18 degrees in boracite, producing contrast equal and opposite to that of the polarisation. Kikuchi band contrast is the only signal that reports absolute polarity without knowledge of the specimen thickness, but it does so only up to 0.09 degrees in PbTiO3, 0.015 degrees in BaTiO3 and 0.02 degrees in boracite. From these results we define tilt tolerances for each signal and material, and propose practical criteria for distinguishing polarisation contrast from misorientation. The analysis also applies to scanning electron microscopy-based diffraction, including electron backscatter diffraction.

papers.title: On generalized $k$-token graphs with distinguishable tokens and a maximum capacity of $s$ tokens per vertex
papers.abstract: Supertoken graphs \(F^s_{k\times1}(G)\), also known as generalized token graphs, model configurations of \(k\) distinguishable tokens on a graph \(G\), with at most \(s\) tokens at each vertex. We study structural and metric properties of these graphs in terms of the base graph. For regular \(G\), we characterize when \(F^s_{k\times1}(G)\) is regular. We show that bipartiteness is inherited from \(G\) and characterize it for complete base graphs. For \(s\ge2\), we characterize connectedness and show that \(t\)-vertex-connectivity of \(G\) implies \(t\)-vertex-connectivity of the supertoken graph. We obtain exact diameter formulas in several regimes, including complete graphs and stars, and derive lower bounds and a conjectured formula for odd cycles. We also determine the clique number, give bounds and equality conditions for the chromatic number, and characterize planarity for complete base graphs.

papers.title: Classification of radially symmetric solutions to a Hardy-H{é}non equation with sublinear absorption and applications
papers.abstract: Uniqueness of a non-negative radially symmetric solution with non-increasing profile to the Hardy-H{é}non elliptic equation with sublinear absorption \\ ____________ $Δ$v(x) + |x|\textsuperscript{$σ$}v(x) - v\textsuperscript{1/m}(x)=0, ______ x$\in$___\textsuperscript{N}, \\ is established in the range N$\ge$1, m>1 and $σ$$\in$(max{-2,-N},0). Consequences of this result are the uniqueness (up to scaling) of the non-negative extremal function to a Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg inequality and the uniqueness of a non-negative radially symmetric self-similar solution with nonincreasing profile to a parabolic Hardy-H{é}non equation with quasilinear diffusion. The proof relies on ordinary differential equations techniques, which can be used thanks to the radially symmetric setting, and requires in particular a delicate analysis of the well-posedness and continuous dependence in view of the non-Lipschitz nonlinearity and the singularity of |x|\textsuperscript{$σ$} at the origin.

papers.title: An All-Atom Model of the Resorcinol-Formaldehyde Aerogel Skeleton from DFT and Molecular Dynamics: Validation and Iron Incorporation
papers.abstract: Resorcinol-formaldehyde (RF) aerogels are lightweight, ultra-porous thermal superinsulators whose complex amorphous structure has not yet been described at the all-atom level. Here, we build an all-atom model of the RF aerogel skeleton by combining density functional theory (DFT) and classical molecular dynamics (MD), validate it against experimental infrared and density measurements, and use it to study the incorporation of iron dopants. The RF base unit was optimized with Gaussian, DMol$^{3}$ and SIESTA, and its calculated infrared spectrum agreed with experiment. Comparing classical force fields with DFT for branched systems of two to four base units (140-278 atoms) led to the choice of COMPASS II. A 15,012-atom system of 54 branched RF units, not cross-linked to each other, aggregated into a single cluster in the canonical (NVT) ensemble and reached an equilibrium density of 1.296 g.cm$^{-3}$ in the isobaric-isothermal (NPT) ensemble, in agreement with the experimental skeletal density (1.3 g.cm$^{-3}$). Then, 5 wt$\%$ iron (109 atoms) was added to the equilibrated structure: during 1 ns of NPT simulation, the fraction of iron atoms embedded in the skeleton rose from 63$\%$ to 71$\%$, and the Fe-C radial distribution function peaked at 3 Å. The model thus provides an experimentally supported starting point for screening fillers and dopants in RF gels, with prospective application to their thermoelectric functionalization, which we have previously demonstrated experimentally with basalt and PANOX fibres. Future extensions could address skeleton properties relevant to thermal insulation and the pyrolysis of RF gels into carbon and metal-doped carbon aerogels.

papers.title: Uniqueness of the hexagonal lattice's universal optimality
papers.abstract: We build on a recent proof of the universal optimality of the planar hexagonal lattice. We extend this result to demonstrate that, up to Euclidean motion, the hexagonal lattice is the only periodic configuration with this property.

papers.title: A Design Rule for Passive Reconfigurable Microwave Devices
papers.abstract: Every reconfigurable microwave device places a tuning element - a varactor, a diode, transistor, microelectromechanical or phase-change switch, a ferroelectric or liquid-crystal load - inside a fixed passive network. The network can make a small change of the element produce a large change of the response, and design practice often credits it with the device's tuning capability. This paper shows that a fixed, linear, passive network cannot add to that capability. Each tuning element carries a tuning budget, a dimensionless length computed from its own impedance trajectory, and a fixed passive network can transmit that budget or lose part of it, never enlarge it. The unit of the budget is the hyperbolic distance of the Smith chart: the distance from a match is the logarithm of the voltage standing-wave ratio, and the distance between two states sets their mutual mismatch and is the logarithm of their commutation quality factor. From one inequality we derive closed-form, ready-to-use limits for analog and digital phase shifters, true-time-delay lines, switches, attenuators, vector modulators, impedance tuners, tunable filters, reconfigurable antennas, metasurface cells and multiport networks; the two-state and attenuation limits are attained by explicit circuits, and the phase limit by a constant-loss trajectory. We introduce the $Λ$-chart, a Smith-chart companion on which budgets and requirements are read graphically, and apply it to four published microwave case studies.

papers.title: DyPSI: Dynamic Physics Sensing via Joint Field and Sensor-Trajectory Generation
papers.abstract: Physics sensing in evolving environments requires reconstructing dense spatiotemporal fields from sparse observations while adapting where future observations should be collected. Existing reconstruction and sensor-placement methods have made substantial progress, but they typically rely on static sensing assumptions: they either use a single layout across all frames or optimize placements independently at each frame, which limits their ability to produce temporally coherent sensing trajectories. We introduce DyPSI, a dynamic physics sensing framework that formulates this problem as the joint generation of future fields and sensor trajectories conditioned on historical observations. DyPSI lifts discrete sensor coordinates into continuous Sensor Position Fields, encodes fields and sensing configurations with a shared Functional Tucker representation, and trains a joint diffusion model to generate future fields and sensing trajectories simultaneously in the resulting latent space. A Gaussian-process temporal kernel correlates the perturbation injected during diffusion training, biasing the denoiser toward temporally smooth recoveries, and we further provide an analysis linking the EDM training objective to a sequence-aggregated A-optimality criterion and a kernel-induced bound on discrete trajectory variation. Experiments on turbulent flow, GLORYS12 sea-surface temperature, and 3D car aerodynamics show that DyPSI consistently outperforms static and frame-wise placement strategies, with substantial error reduction under tight sensor budgets. The code is available at https://github.com/mengqi132/DyPSI.

papers.title: Building a Method: Challenges and Lessons from Developing an Impact Evaluation Framework for Public Investment in Open Source Software
papers.abstract: Modern societies and institutions depend on an invisible layer of open digital infrastructure: foundational, openly accessible digital technologies that support a broad range of social and economic activities. Open source software is a core component of this infrastructure, underpinning everyday technologies and critical systems in various critical sectors. As open source software becomes increasingly recognised, funded, and governed as open digital infrastructure, policymakers face growing demands for accountability, transparency, and credible evidence of impact. However, methods for evaluating public investment in open source software remain underdeveloped, with no widely accepted methodological standard. This paper describes the Sovereign Tech Agency's transition from qualitative reporting and funding-recipient self-assessment towards a mixed-methods approach that incorporates quantitative, goal-oriented evaluation to inform funding decisions. Drawing on the development of this framework, it examines its initial design, the practical and structural challenges encountered, and the responses adopted. The work identifies three central challenges: evaluation indicators must reflect heterogeneous project goals and contexts; quantitative assessment relies on fragmented and fragile data infrastructure; and observed changes before, during, and after investment do not establish causal attribution without additional research designs. The paper argues that evaluating investment in open source software is not only a methodological task but also a governance practice, dependent on sustainable open research infrastructure, community knowledge, and ongoing methodological refinement.

papers.title: MonoLaDN: Language-Guided DeNoising for Monocular 3D Object Detection
papers.abstract: Monocular 3D object detection offers a low-cost route to 3D perception, but it remains fundamentally ill-posed, since depth must be inferred from a single view. Recent transformer-based detectors learn geometry purely from image features and 3D box annotations, lacking the high-level semantic priors that vision-language models (VLMs) acquire from large-scale pretraining. VLMs offer such priors, but deploying one directly as a detector is impractical due to its heavy inference cost. We propose MonoLaDN, a language-guided denoising framework that transfers the geometric reasoning of a VLM into a monocular 3D detector while keeping the deployed model purely vision-based. During training, a frozen VLM produces structured reasoning about each object's occlusion, depth, dimension, and angle from the image and its ground-truth boxes. We encode this reasoning into queries, perturb them with noise, and train the detector to reconstruct the clean reasoning. Reconstructing the corrupted reasoning forces the detector's depth-guided features to internalize the VLM's geometric priors, so this knowledge remains available even after the reasoning path is discarded at inference, adding no latency or parameters to the deployed model. Experiments on KITTI 3D and nuScenes show that MonoLaDN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art detectors and generalizes well to new domains.

papers.title: All reweighted paths lead to Rome: Unification of reweighting schemes for stratified path sampling
papers.abstract: Path sampling-based stratification algorithms such as Transition Interface Sampling (TIS) enable the evaluation of kinetic rate constants and mechanisms of complex molecular rare event transitions. By sampling only short dynamical trajectories, TIS allows constructing an estimate of the unbiased dynamics by reweighting the interface path ensembles. In the past decades several methods have been developed and applied to achieve such path reweighting, based on statistically optimal use of the trajectory data. Why and how this reweighting exactly works has been underexplored up to now. Here we discuss several different schemes to compute the reweighted path ensemble (RPE), notably point-wise matching, Weighted Histogram Analysis Method (WHAM), Multistate Bennett Acceptance Ratio (MBAR), variance based reweighting (VBR) and survival analysis reweighting (SAR). We show that except for the point-wise matching the other methods are leading to the same outcome, and in fact can be seen as identical. Moreover, the SAR links to a well-established nonparametric maximum-likelihood estimator of product-limit form. This allows a synthesis of all path reweighting schemes, identifying the common underlying nature. All schemes follow from this common origin. We illustrate the reweighting with some simple examples, and show that care has to be taken when applying WHAM, if the number of interfaces and histogram bins do not match.

papers.title: A search for sterile neutrinos at ultrahigh energies at the Pierre Auger Observatory
papers.abstract: We investigate the sensitivity of the Pierre Auger Observatory to sterile neutrinos with masses in the MeV-to-100 MeV range. To this end, we consider a minimal $3+1$ framework in which a single sterile state mixes mainly with the $ν_τ$ flavor through an active--sterile mixing angle $θ_N$ to produce a mass eigenstate $N_1$. At ultrahigh energies, $N_1$ neutrinos can traverse substantial chord lengths through the Earth and interact through their active component, producing $τ$ leptons that may emerge near the surface and decay in the atmosphere, thereby generating detectable air showers. We compute the corresponding exposures with a detailed Monte Carlo simulation of neutrino propagation, interactions, $τ$ energy losses and decay, and derive upper limits at $90\%$ confidence level on an isotropic diffuse flux of $N_1$ neutrinos. For an $E^{-2}$ spectrum, we obtain $E^2Φ_N\leq 2\times10^{-9}\sin^{-2}θ_N\,\mathrm{GeV\,cm^{-2}\,sr^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$ over $0.3$--$200$ EeV for $\sin^2θ_N\lesssim10^{-1}$. We further consider $N_1$ neutrinos arising from the decay of a superheavy dark-matter particle. For a benchmark dark-matter mass of $10^{13}$ GeV, we derive constraints on the active--sterile mixing angle and dark-matter lifetime for sterile-neutrino masses of $10$ and $100$ MeV. These results illustrate the potential of the Observatory to probe long-lived weakly interacting particles.
authors: J. R. T. de Mello Neto

papers.title: Virtual Microphone Array for Direction-of-Arrival Estimation Based on Fiber-Optic Position Sensing
papers.abstract: This paper presents a virtual microphone array approach for estimating the direction of arrival of a sound source using a moving microphone and a stationary reference microphone. The method exploits the microphone motion to generate a time-varying array geometry, using fiber-optic position sensing to reconstruct the trajectory and determine the resulting virtual microphone configurations. For each configuration, the estimated time difference of arrival between the two microphone signals and the corresponding microphone geometry define a hyperboloid representing all possible sound source positions consistent with the time difference. By combining multiple hyperboloid constraints, the direction of arrival can be estimated in azimuth and elevation relative to the microphone coordinate system. In contrast to conventional arrays with fixed geometries and approaches based on predefined microphone trajectories, the proposed method derives the virtual array geometry directly from the measured microphone motion, enabling a spatially distributed virtual array to be formed using only two physical microphones and offering potential for size- and weight-constrained applications. The approach was experimentally evaluated under controlled low-reflection conditions for different source positions, source distances, and signal characteristics. The influence of microphone motion was further examined, and the method was tested with a moving sound source. The results demonstrate the feasibility of direction-of-arrival estimation using a virtual microphone array without requiring a predefined microphone trajectory.

papers.title: Clear Human Web: Where a Person Vouches for Every Client
papers.abstract: The web cannot tell whether a request comes from a person or from a program. Sites have checked the network address and puzzles in its place, and both have given way: automated traffic exceeds human traffic, and puzzles are solved for pay and by agents. This paper proposes the Clear Human Web, the part of the public web that sites open only to clients a person vouches for. A person's wallet presents their person identification data (PID) to one issuer, the only party that registers as a relying party, and receives a bounded number of blind-signed tokens, proofs of personhood that carry no attribute. The browser spends one token at each site that runs the gate, and the site learns that a valid token of a trusted issuer was spent, and nothing else. No field is added to the PID, no protocol is introduced, no site registers, and the publisher of a site holds the same proof as its readers. We define the Clear Human Web through five properties and seven adversaries, and state which properties the construction satisfies against each adversary. The identities a person can hold on one site in an epoch are bounded to k. The bound holds once the wallet limits a person to one pseudonym at the issuer. In the optimum k = 1, and a zero-knowledge proof of PID possession and a pseudonym per site replace the tokens.

papers.title: Corridor-Based Monitoring and Emergency Braking Decision for Automated Vehicle Safety
papers.abstract: This paper addresses emergency-braking decisions for a redundant safety channel in automated vehicles. The channel is responsible for identifying hazards from sensor data and determining whether braking is necessary, given the constrained computational resources of embedded hardware. We present an emergency-braking approach that uses a predicted motion corridor to filter \ac{lidar} measurements and then decide whether the ego vehicle must brake. \ac{pmcm} constructs a curvature-aware boundary from the planned path and vehicle geometry so that the monitored region contains the full swept body on both straight and curved paths. \ac{gdeta} then decides whether the ego vehicle must command an emergency brake for objects inside this boundary, scoring geometric occupancy and temporal urgency independently. Hard gates permit braking when either source is conclusive; soft-OR arbitration combines partial evidence when neither gate is active. Consecutive-scan confirmation reduces sensitivity to transient measurement noise. Corridor coverage is evaluated in controlled collision simulations and recorded campus driving. Braking decisions are evaluated in Monte Carlo simulations of lead-vehicle braking and transverse-crossing encounters.

papers.title: Optimal stability estimates and preasymptotic error analysis of the CIP-FEM for the Helmholtz equation with uniaxial perfectly matched layers
papers.abstract: We study the uniaxial perfectly matched layer (UPML) problem for the Helmholtz equation in two and three dimensions and establish wavenumber-explicit stability estimates at high wavenumbers. For the full-space UPML problem, we prove the optimal stability estimate with the inf-sup constant satisfying $μ_\infty\eqsim k^{-1}$ for sufficiently large $k$ if the absorption function $σ\in W^{1,\infty}$ is a piecewise-power function of order at least one for which $\|σ'\|_{L^\infty(\{t:0<σ(t)\leqδ_*\})}\leq \varepsilon_*$, where $\varepsilon_*$ and $δ_*$ depend only on the PML parameters. Using this stability estimate, we obtain the optimal inf-sup estimate $μ_L\eqsim k^{-1}$ for the truncated UPML problem. These estimates further yield preasymptotic error estimates for a linear continuous interior penalty finite element method (CIP-FEM). Numerical simulations confirmed the theoretical predictions and demonstrated the effectiveness of CIP-FEM under high-wavenumber conditions.

papers.title: AGORA cities: the hidden infrastructure shaping urban fragility
papers.abstract: Urban services are unevenly distributed across the city, yet it is unclear when their joint presence signals fragility and when it instead outlines a neighbourhood's vocation. For Bologna and Florence, we integrate Foursquare and OpenStreetMap points of interest with Sentinel-2-derived green indicators based on the 3-30-300 rule, cluster urban areas accordingly, and benchmark the clusters against the demographic, social, economic and composite fragility indices produced by the municipal statistical offices, which are exogenous to the analysis. In both cities, we identify a subset of infrastructures, termed AGORA (Arts, Green environments, and Open Routes for Access and mobility), whose joint provision is associated with lower fragility. The AGORA Alignment score (AA), based on the rank correlation between AGORA endowment and composite fragility, indicates full alignment in Florence (AA = 1.00) and strong but incomplete alignment in Bologna (AA = 0.80). The remaining service categories instead show wide and heterogeneous distributions: they differentiate areas without tracking fragility and can be interpreted as expressions of urban vocations. The least fragile cluster, the only one with full AGORA endowment, hosts just 3.3% of residents in Bologna and 6.3% in Florence. The framework offers a procedure transferable to other contexts and identifies the expansion of AGORA infrastructures as a candidate lever for reducing fragility without altering existing vocations.

papers.title: The Split Protocol Decides the Result: Re-Evaluating Encrypted Traffic Classification
papers.abstract: Encrypted traffic classifiers are routinely reported at 95-99% accuracy. We show that on one of two public corpora, the same model and code score macro-F1 0.992 under the evaluation protocol standard in the literature and 0.567 under a protocol that keeps flows from one packet capture on one side of the split. Nothing changes but the partition (gap 0.426 over eight seeds, p = 0.008 after Holm-Bonferroni correction). The inflation is not a property of random splitting as such. On a month of backbone QUIC traffic, we evaluate five split protocols at eight seeds each: random, temporal and client-disjoint splitting are statistically indistinguishable from session-disjoint, while server-disjoint splitting costs 0.192 macro-F1 (d = 17.0, p = 0.008). Which axis matters depends on how the corpus was collected, in a way invisible from its label space. We give a diagnostic that identifies the right axis before any model is trained: single-identifier probes. A decision tree on the capture identifier alone reaches 0.983 under a random split and exactly 0.000 under session-disjoint splitting. Under this evaluation, a metric-trained flow embedding leads four deep baselines but does not beat gradient-boosted trees on twenty packet sizes. Five of our own pre-registered architectural claims fail: distance-based rejection of unknown applications beats softmax thresholding, but ablating every metric objective makes rejection better, because class separation correlates at r = -0.88 with rejection quality. Few-shot enrollment is flat within a corpus but, across corpora, five labelled flows per class recover 91% of the deficit left by failed zero-shot transfer. All splits, results, code and negative findings are released.

papers.title: Bridging Pulse and Circuit Levels: A Geometric Framework for Deterministic Error Suppression
papers.abstract: Quantum errors in noisy environments remain a major obstacle to advancing quantum information technology. Standard quantum error correction requires massive ancillary qubit overhead, motivating the need for hardware-efficient mitigation strategies. In this work, we propose a framework for dynamical quantum error correction at the circuit level, requiring no logical encoding or ancillary qubits. By extending a geometric framework (originally developed for creating dynamical error-correcting gates at the control pulse level) to the discrete dynamics of digital circuits, we map the accumulation of coherent errors to trajectories in a high-dimensional error space. We demonstrate that inserting deterministically optimized twirling gate sequences actively shapes these trajectories, utilizing destructive interference to keep the accumulated error bounded with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(1)$. This deterministic path-shaping suppresses circuit errors fundamentally differently than the stochastic random-walk behavior of standard randomized compiling with error scaling $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$. Furthermore, we show that this circuit-level dynamical correction synergizes with pulse-level robust control, providing an analytical bridge between continuous noise dynamics and discrete quantum compilation. This research illuminates pathways to achieving highly noise-resistant quantum circuits prior to the era of fault tolerance.

papers.title: Entire solutions of a special binomial differential equation
papers.abstract: We consider the binomial differential equation $$ ff'-a(f'')^2=be^{2c},$$ where $a(z)$, $b(z)$, $c(z)$ are polynomials such that $b(z)\not\equiv 0$ and $c(z)$ is non-constant. In this paper, we determine all entire solutions of this equation.

papers.title: A Construction Framework for Three-Dimensional Topological Magnetic Textures
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional magnetic systems offer diverse possibilities for constructing complex topological textures from simpler magnetic configurations. Here, we present different routes for constructing complex three-dimensional magnetic textures from simpler parent configurations and discuss their impact on the topology of the resulting structures. We identify four construction principles: (i) adding transverse modulations, (ii) adding structures, (iii) entangling textures (e.g. braiding, or twisting), and (iv) introducing singularities. Using the skyrmion tube as an explicit parent configuration, we show how these principles give rise to several known three-dimensional magnetic textures. We then apply the same principles to predict novel textures derived from a meron tube, which are confirmed by micromagnetic simulations to be metastable in chiral magnets. Our results establish general principles for the systematic construction and discovery of complex three-dimensional magnetic textures.

papers.title: When Can Self-Play Fix a False Belief? Answer Keys, Pass Bands and Replacement Rules in an Execution-Grounded Loop
papers.abstract: Self-play loops in which a model writes tasks, derives an answer key and trains on its own matching solutions are often called grounded when the key comes from executing code. We ask which false beliefs such a loop removes. We run expert-iteration self-play with Qwen3-4B-Base on output-prediction tasks, vary the source of the answer key, and track natural beliefs about Python semantics and two misreadings of task specifications planted by fine-tuning ("at most n" read as < n; "the k-th smallest" read as 0-indexed). Executing the generator's own code gave a key that encoded the "at most" misreading on every audited task, and training on it never raised the truth rate above 0.03. A key from an implementation by the unplanted model, a teacher without the error, raised it to 0.23-0.58 after three rounds in four runs. A correct key is not sufficient: the pass band, which keeps tasks solved 1-7 times of 8, admits almost no corrective task while a belief is held on nearly every sample. Execution keys sharply reduced both natural runtime beliefs on diagnostic items in both seeds. Corrections came with replacement rules that fail on neighbouring items the old belief got right. The robust case, present in all four spec runs, is that after the "at most" fix the model increasingly counts the nearest value above a limit that is absent from the list (overcount 0.18-0.38 of control samples at round 3), a case our planted generators almost never wrote (4 of 10,924 tasks); diagnostic-only metrics miss it. Asked for those cases, the planted generator wrote none in 2,061 checkable tasks, against 27% for the untrained unplanted model in one round. Both generators often moved the request into the specification instead ("the cap itself does not count"), and a decorrelated key follows the specification.

papers.title: A.S.E 2.0: Understanding How Repository Context Impacts the Security of LLM-Generated Code
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding assistants and agents construct a repository context before generating code. For security-sensitive code, this context decides whether the model sees the project's safeguards (e.g., authorization checks) or insecure code to imitate. However, context construction is designed almost exclusively for functional correctness, and secure-code benchmarks treat the context as fixed, so how repository context affects the security of generated code remains unclear. We construct CASE-Bench, a benchmark of 145 repository-level tasks from real CVEs in 51 projects. Each task runs in Docker, has functional tests and a proof-of-concept exploit validated in both directions, and is annotated with the repository code that enforces or undermines its security. Using CASE-Bench, we compare 13 context construction methods and six controls with six LLMs, edit single context elements, and analyze coding-agent trajectories. We find that (1) functionality-oriented context raises the functional pass rate by up to 8.2 percentage points (pp) but the secure pass rate by at most 3.7 pp, (2) withholding a safeguard lowers the secure pass rate by up to 8.1 pp, while one inserted insecure exemplar raises correct-but-exploitable code by 6.3 pp, and (3) coding agents observe the relevant safeguard in only 27-36% of trajectories. These findings inform security-aware context construction and secure-code evaluation.

papers.title: Spectral flow in AdS$\mathbf{_3}$ revisited
papers.abstract: We revisit an old idea that spectral flow in WZW models can be associated with certain $G$-bundles over a worldsheet. This allows us to introduce a novel method for computing correlators of spectrally-flowed vertex operators in WZW models with group $G$ and level $k$, by systematically computing the contribution from a network of line defects. Specialising to the case of $G=SL(2, \mathbb{R})$, as is relevant to AdS$_3$ string theory, we demonstrate that generic $n$-point functions of spectrally-flowed vertex operators at tree level can be rewritten in terms of an $(n+1)$-point function of $n$ unflowed vertex operators and one degenerate insertion. This is to be interpreted as an unflowed $n$-point function in an instanton background. Moreover, we conjecture that this $(n+1)$-point function can be recast as an $n$-point function of unflowed operators and we provide evidence for this. We demonstrate that the $(n+1)$-point function satisfies the same constraints from global spacetime conformal invariance as does an unflowed $n$-point function for a specific choice of spacetime coordinates that we determine. We verify that our results agree with bootstrap results in the literature. This provides the next step towards fully solving the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ WZW model.

papers.title: Multi-Resident Data Association in Smart Homes via MDP Modeling and Behavior Cloning
papers.abstract: Ambient sensors offer a privacy-preserving solution for activity recognition in smart homes, yet they face a critical challenge in multi-resident environments known as Data Association, which aims to identify the resident triggering a specific anonymous sensor event. Existing approaches fundamentally fail to maintain global consistency by often yielding conflicting associations for silent residents. Additionally, these methods frequently suffer from severe trajectory fragmentation caused by the ontological mismatch of applying continuous physical motion models to discrete logical behaviors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework that reformulates data association as a sequential decision-making task within a Markov Decision Process (MDP). We solve the defined MDP via Behavior Cloning (BC) to avoid complex reward engineering by directly learning from expert demonstrations. We instantiate the policy using two complementary architectures, including a lightweight Transformer that treats association as a multi-label classification task over linearized event histories, and a fine-tuned Large Language Model (LLM) that reformulates the problem as conditional text generation to leverage pre-trained semantic knowledge. Extensive evaluations on three diverse datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in resolving concurrent multi-resident events. Furthermore, the LLM-based policy shows preliminary cross-environment transfer potential under benchmark settings, while its robustness in real deployments still requires further validation.

papers.title: Speaker-Consistent Grounding for Confusion-Resilient LLM-Based Target Speech Extraction
papers.abstract: Deterministic target-speaker extraction (TSE) tends to preserve observed linguistic content but may extract the interfering speaker. In contrast, autoregressive generative TSE improves perceptual quality, but is prone to content hallucination and speaker identity drift, which can be mitigated by model grounding with the evidence from the deterministic TSE. However, grounding such a generative TSE model with speaker-confused evidence may therefore reinforce the error. To address this gap, we proposed a repair-before-grounding framework with a training-free evidence-repair stage. Conditioning-diverse candidate selection (CDCS) selects target speaker-consistent evidence from complementary frozen TSE outputs. The selected waveform can then be used by code-space grounding (CSG) to constrain LLM-based TSE decoding. On Libri2Mix, CDCS reduces wrong-speaker extraction errors from 6.87% to 0.75% on clean mixtures and from 18.95% to 10.46% under noise. With the LLM-based TSE checkpoint unchanged, CSG further reduces noisy content- and acoustic-switch rates from 12.79% and 1.68% to 9.10% and 0.51%, respectively. Despite this stronger grounding, generative TSE retains its predicted perceptual-quality advantage over direct deterministic extraction. These results show that repairing evidence identity before grounding improves the reliability of generative TSE. Audio demos and code are available at https://hanyu-meng.github.io/LLM-TSE-Grounding-Demo/.

papers.title: Critical one-arm probabilities for metric-graph loop soups in dimensions $d\ge3$
papers.abstract: We study the critical Brownian loop soup on the metric graph $\widetilde{\mathbb Z}^d$. Using a new unified approach, we determine the one-arm probability up to multiplicative constants in all dimensions $d\ge3$. In particular, at the upper critical dimension $d_c=6$, we show that the one-arm probability is comparable to $r^{-2}(\log r)^{\frac12}$, and moreover, with high probability a box of radius $r$ contains on the order of $\log r$ macroscopic clusters, each with volume of order $r^4(\log r)^{-\frac12}$. For $d\ne6$, we recover the one-arm estimates of Cai and Ding, $r^{-(d-2)/2}$ for $d=3,4,5$ and $r^{-2}$ for $d>6$ (arXiv:2406.02397; Probab. Theory Relat. Fields, 2025), and the three-dimensional estimate of Drewitz, Prévost and Rodriguez (Probab. Theory Relat. Fields, 2026). Our proof adapts the entropy method of Dewan and Muirhead (Probab. Theory Relat. Fields, 2023) to the loop-soup setting. This yields a renormalization inequality for the one-arm probability, from which we derive the upper bounds. Independently, Rodriguez, Shi, and Zhang (arXiv:2611.05357) have recently used a closely related entropy approach to recover the one-arm estimates for $d>6$ and improve the upper bound for $d=6$. They also announce the same sharp one-arm estimate for $d=6$ in forthcoming work.

papers.title: STEK: Structural-Terrain-Enhanced Koopman-Inspired Cross-Channel Regularization for Retrospective Battery Multi-Target Estimation
papers.abstract: Retrospective battery characterization across heterogeneous cells is challenging because cycling records vary substantially with chemistry, protocol, cell format, capacity, and operating conditions. An endpoint charge--discharge curve captures the local condition of an evaluated cycle, while a cell-level lifecycle terrain summarizes structural evolution across the archived trajectory. We propose STEK, a structural-terrain-enhanced framework for retrospective battery multi-target estimation. STEK combines a cell-level lifecycle (dQ/dV) terrain with an endpoint-derived structural proxy through quality-proxy-conditioned gating. Bounded FiLM and a validity-gated residual head refine the endpoint-curve representation while preserving a curve-based prediction pathway. Battery-type and optional material-text representations further condition an identity-centered low-rank linear map, providing a Koopman-inspired cross-channel consistency objective without modeling temporal dynamics or performing rollout. Under the fixed seven-output MIX-battery protocol, the full retrospective setting improves aggregate performance over endpoint-only learned baselines across multiple temporal backbones; this comparison reflects both the additional archived context and the modeling design. Under matched auxiliary inputs, STEK outperforms direct concatenation and quality-unaware FiLM, while descriptor-removal tests show graceful fallback to the endpoint pathway. Deterministic rules remain preferable for directly recoverable capacity summaries. The method targets retrospective archive harmonization rather than online estimation from cycle t alone.

papers.title: Perfect Forms and Torsion Bounds in Algebraic $K$-Theory over Totally Real and CM Fields
papers.abstract: We extend the method of Van Woerden \cite{woerden} to totally real and CM number fields to obtain an upper bound for the number of $\GLo-$equivalence classes of perfect forms. Moreover, by considering appropriate barycentric subdivisions of the Voronoi tessellation, we extend these estimates to the number of $\GLo$-orbits of $k$-dimensional faces of the Voronoi tessellation. As a consequence, we improve the asymptotic order of the bounds for the torsion part of $K_m(\rint)$ obtained by Soulé \cite{soule_hermitian_bounds} and Houriet \cite{Juliet_PHD}. We emphasise the improvement of the general bound for $F=\mathbb Q$, unchanged since Soulé's work, and the independence of the discriminant exponent from the field degree for totally real and CM fields.

papers.title: Multiple $q$-zeta values as polynomials in partition multiplicities
papers.abstract: Writing multiple $q$-zeta values as sums over partitions, a conjecture of Bachmann, proved by Hirose, Maesaka and Watanabe by means of a recursion, says that polynomials in the parts and multiplicities can be replaced by polynomials in the multiplicities alone. We make this replacement explicit, derive from it bounds on weight and depth that make Bachmann's conjecture effective, and provide a closed formula for the Drop1 operator of Hirose, Maesaka, Seki and Watanabe.

papers.title: Beyond Scene Shortcuts: Action-Centric Video-Text Alignment for Fine-Grained Action Understanding
papers.abstract: Fine-grained action understanding requires vision-language models to ground what an agent does, how it acts, and why it acts in spatio-temporal evidence. However, richer supervision can backfire: fine-tuned models may generate detailed action descriptions grounded in static scenes and salient objects rather than motion, a failure we call Environment-Grounded Action Hallucination (EGAH). To mitigate EGAH, we propose Staged Attention Rectification and Reinforcement (STARR), an action-centric video-text alignment framework that breaks scene-action shortcuts through Action-Environment Dissociation and reinforces action-focused grounding with an Attention Consistency Reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization. We further construct FineActionR&R, combining temporally localized captions with hierarchical and temporal-causal reasoning data. Built on Qwen2.5-VL-7B, FineActionVLM-R1 improves average MotionBench accuracy by 3.01 percentage points over its base model and achieves 91.50% on HAU-MCQ-Bench. Qualitative comparisons further indicate more faithful fine-grained action descriptions with fewer environment-induced hallucinations.

papers.title: An Engineering Reading of the Bounded Halting Problem and Observable Properties of a Universal Machine
papers.abstract: The halting problem asks whether a program eventually halts, with unrestricted resources. Engineering systems instead certify bounded halting: given a program, an input, and a step budget T, decide whether the program halts within T steps. This paper studies two of its uses. First, it defines an exact finite-budget problem, placing the simulated program and the checker on the same unit-cost timescale, so the checker can be embedded in an adversarial program. A diagonal argument with explicit additive overhead shows that no fixed deterministic checker decides every instance within any fixed fraction of T below one, for large T. In the nondeterministic case, T bounds the branch depth allowed for a stable observable decision. Second, bounded-halting instances give adversarial tests for finitary universality, since a universal model must support arbitrary finite computations as T grows. The tests check resource growth with T, the absence of a fixed deliberation bound, and later access to intermediate data. They separate a fixed model with extendable external resources, a model family that grows with T, and a larger system built around a fixed component. For machine-learning systems, this identifies the resource growth a universality claim assumes and whether it fails for deployed models.

papers.title: Euclid: Survey mask effects on clustering of galaxy clusters
papers.abstract: Wide-area cluster catalogues from Stage-IV surveys will substantially improve the precision of cluster clustering measurements, making the control of observational systematic effects essential for cosmological inference. In preparation for the first Euclid data release (DR1), we assess the impact of the survey mask and non-homogeneous sky coverage on the two-point correlation function of galaxy clusters and its covariance. Using DR1-like lightcone mocks, we confirm that the irregular footprint does not introduce appreciable changes in the two-point correlation function when the same mask is applied to the random catalogue. We also find that spatial inhomogeneities, implemented as variations of the cluster selection function in different patches of the sky, do not significantly bias the clustering amplitude, up to levels of variation well above those expected for DR1. When the degree of inhomogeneity is increased to the regime where the effect becomes significant, we show that its amplitude is related to the maximum variation of the selection function among different regions, rather than to the number of such regions. We further find that irregular mask geometry and non-uniform sky coverage both increase the clustering covariance, introducing small, nearly scale-independent offsets that can be captured by nuisance parameters in the covariance model. Our results consolidate the treatment of mask systematic errors for DR1 and inform the methodological refinements required for future \Euclid cluster cosmology.

papers.title: Identities of Representation of Lie subalgebras of the first Weyl algebra
papers.abstract: Let $F$ be a field. We study weak polynomial identities for pairs $(A,V)$ where $A$ is the first Weyl algebra over $F$ and $V$ is either a Lie subalgebra (under the usual Lie bracket) of $A$, or simply a vector subspace of $A$. Sometimes the weak identities of $(A,V)$, when $V$ is a Lie algebra, are called identities of representations of Lie algebras. Our starting point is the description of finite dimensional Lie algebras $L$ that can be embedded into the first Weyl algebra; this description was given by Rausch de Traubenberg, Slupinski and Tanasă in 2006. First we assume that $F$ is algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, and describe a finite basis of the weak identities of the pair $(A,L)$ where $L=\mathfrak{sl}_2$. In order to obtain such a basis we invoke theorems by Razmyslov and by Trishin concerning the identities of infinite dimensional irreducible representations of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$. Afterwards we consider $L$ as a filiform Lie algebra together with its concrete realisation inside the first Weyl algebra. We produce a finite basis of weak identities of the pair $(A,L)$, assuming $F$ to be infinite. Finally we study the weakest form of identities for $(A,V)$ where $A$ is the $n$-th Weyl algebra and $V$ is just a vector space - its canonical generating vector subspace. We deduce a basis of the weak identities in this case as well, once again assuming $F$ to be an infinite field, with no restriction on its characteristic. The same result was recently obtained by Dotsenko and Lopatin in characteristic $0$ by different methods. Our methods are combinatorial, we also use the theory developed by Razmyslov, and the representations of the symmetric and the general linear groups and their duality. We employ the characteristic-free description of the invariants of the symplectic group given by De Concini and Procesi.

papers.title: Spatial Path Superposition: A No-Cloning Perspective on MIMO-Inspired Spatial Diversity
papers.abstract: Spatial diversity is a key mechanism in classical Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) communications, where multiple propagation alternatives provide redundant observations that improve reliability in noisy environments. A direct translation of this principle to quantum communications is forbidden by the no-cloning theorem, since an unknown quantum state cannot be copied and transmitted through independent links. In this Perspective article, we argue that spatial path superposition provides a no-cloning-compatible analogue of the spatial-diversity principle of MIMO. Rather than duplicating the transmitted quantum state, a quantum carrier is coherently delocalized over multiple communication links, so that alternative spatial evolutions are experienced in quantum superposition. In this framework, classical redundancy is replaced by spatial coherence, and the communication link itself becomes part of the quantum dynamics. Indeed, spatial coherence can enhance the fidelity of the received quantum state, providing the quantum counterpart of the classical diversity gain, and can be converted into bipartite and multipartite entanglement during propagation. This implies that, under suitable coherent path control, noisy channel evolutions can contribute constructively to entanglement generation. This Perspective identifies spatial path superposition as a quantum-native primitive for the Quantum Internet, linking no-cloning-compatible spatial diversity, fidelity enhancement, entanglement generation, and coherent path control.

papers.title: When Does Risk-Controlled Throughput Forecasting Actually Control Risk? A Reproduction Study on LEO Satellite Link
papers.abstract: Risk-budgeted throughput forecasting converts a point forecast of LEO satellite capacity into a conservative bound whose overestimation rate is held at a user-specified budget, so that admission control can act on it safely. We reproduce the state of the art, BG-CFQS, on the three Starlink traces its authors used and on an independent fourth dataset, and report four findings. First, its risk guarantee is reproducible but conditional on the calibration split: under a random split we recover every published quantity, including risk-pass on 3 of 3 datasets, but under a contiguous temporal split, which is what a deployed terminal faces, it holds on 1 of 3. Second, independent of any split, the method cannot serve a risk budget below 0.15, the low end of its candidate quantile set. On all four datasets the achieved rate is identical at budgets of 0.05, 0.10 and 0.15, overshooting by 1.4x to 3.7x at the tightest. Third, static conformal calibration cannot improve a ranking, only shift an operating point; we confirm this exactly on latency spike detection, where online calibration improves AUPRC by up to 51%. Fourth, group-conditional online recalibration splits into two mechanisms. The online part replicates: it tracks the budget within 1% from 0.05 to 0.35, where static calibration is 16 to 21% off. The group-conditional part does not: on three of four datasets, conditioning on any available covariate, including measured serving-satellite geometry, is worse than not conditioning, and our attempt to predict which datasets benefit failed. What is new here is empirical, not algorithmic: we claim the findings, not the methods.

papers.title: Scale Anchoring via Implicit Semantics and Sequence-Consistent Loop Closure for VGGT-Based SLAM
papers.abstract: Feed-forward geometric foundation models enable dense monocular reconstruction without requiring camera calibration, but independently reconstructed submaps can accumulate scale drift, and even a valid revisit can yield an inconsistent cross-submap measurement. We extend VGGT-SLAM 2.0 with fixed-root scale anchoring and short-sequence-assisted direct loop connections. SALAD selects an image pair between the initial submap and each eligible new submap; joint VGGT inference then uses learned implicit semantic-geometric cues to supply a scale-only anchor while preserving the original overlap chain. For loop closure, neighboring image pairs support a consistency check and translation-scale alignment. Each accepted candidate contributes one robust Sim(3) factor between existing center-frame nodes, without an auxiliary loop submap. A 17-sequence comparison lowers mean Sim(3) ATE on nine TUM sequences from 0.1018 to 0.0451 m relative to the VGGT-SLAM 2.0 baseline. Anchoring improves all seven no-loop module ablations. On three Clio scenes, a fixed-loop comparison favors the direct connection pipeline over the tested auxiliary-submap pipeline. A separate candidate audit exposes additional rejections of visually overlapping pairs by the short-sequence check. These comparisons distinguish the gains from long-range scale anchoring and loop connection choices from the limitations of candidate verification.

papers.title: Large time behavior of global solutions to one-dimensional non-isentropic compressible Navier-Stokes-Poisson equations with large initial data
papers.abstract: In this paper, we are concerned with the construction of global solutions to the Cauchy problem for the one-dimensional non-isentropic compressible Navier-Stokes-Poisson equations, as well as the precise description of their large-time behavior. While results for small initial data are well-established, the case of large initial perturbations remains less satisfactory. Even for constant transport coefficients, only the Nishida-Smoller type solutions have been obtained so far. In this work, we will provide a complete resolution of this problem. The key idea involves revealing favorable hidden identities of the potential force and a new representation for the specific volume, which enables us to derive uniform upper and lower bounds on this quantity. Moreover, this strategy extends to compressible viscous single-ion flow under the Boltzmann relation; notably, this new method for deriving lower and upper bounds on the specific volume also applies to the Navier-Stokes equations. The proof relies on a domain decomposition technique and some new dissipative structures to close the nonlinear energy estimates.

papers.title: Hamiltonicity and cycle factors in k-quasi-transitive digraphs of large diameter
papers.abstract: A digraph is $k$-quasi-transitive if the endpoints of every directed path of length $k$ are adjacent. In this paper, we prove that every strong non-bipartite $k$-quasi-transitive digraph of diameter at least $k+2$ is Hamiltonian when $k\ge7$ is odd. Moreover, combined with the known even case, for $k\ge6$, we also prove that a strong bipartite $k$-quasi-transitive digraph of diameter at least $k+2$ is Hamiltonian if and only if it has a cycle factor. These answer two problems posed by Alva-Samos and Hernández-Cruz affirmatively [Journal of Graph Theory \textbf{96} (2021) 310--325].
